There's a lot of misinformation concerning Ed Snowden's last tweet, which was a checksum for a file. A lot of people seem to think this string of characters is a 'key' of some sort. It is not. A checksum is not a key or a password. A checksum is a device for confirming a file hasn't been tampered with -- it unlocks nothing. It's a verification tool.

The checksum is typically given before a file is transmitted. So that once you receive the file, you can verify that it is in fact the file the sender transmitted and not some modified version of the file that some middle-man has tampered with. If someone changes any part of the file, the checksums will not be the same.

Please don't believe the FUD. It's not a password for the Wikileaks insurance file. It's not a password for anything. To learn more, read about checksums and hashing algorithms.

Because there are a ton of people believing it to be 256-bits, which from the looks of the string, does not seem to be that high at all.

The string is 64-bits. 64=2^6 -- Being a power of two, this strongly suggests this was produced by a hashing algorithm

My guess would be this is a hexadecimal representation of a SHA-256 hash -- One, because it fits and Two, because SHA-256 is one of the most popular hashing functions. It could just as well however, be a 256-bit MD5 hash. Until the file if produced, we're just stabbing in the dark as to which algorithm produced the hash.
